subject: Communication
title: The Splinternet: When the Internet Fragments
description: A 60-second lesson on The Splinternet: When the Internet Fragments.

hook.text: China has its own internet. Russia is building one. The dream of one global connected network is fracturing along.

buildup.text: The 'splinternet' describes the fragmentation of the internet into separate, censored, or regulated networks by.

discovery.text: China's Great Firewall blocks Google, Facebook, and Twitter. 900 million users live in an entirely separate digital reality.

twist.text: Even in 'open' countries, regulations differ: EU privacy laws, US speech protections, and Australia's media bargaining.

climax.text: The splinternet means global media literacy must include understanding which internet you're on — and what you can't see.

punchline.text: There isn't one internet. There are many. And each shows a different world.

quiz.question: What is the 'splinternet'?
options: Fragmentation of the internet along political lines

details.summary: The splinternet describes the fragmentation of the global internet into nationally controlled segments. China's Great Firewall, Russia's sovereign internet law, and the EU's distinct regulations are creating separate digital worlds with different information, rules, and realities.
details.whyItMatters: Internet fragmentation threatens the concept of universal information access and creates populations with fundamentally different digital realities.
takeaways: National governments are creating separate internet segments
China, Russia, and the EU have distinct digital regulations
Fragmentation creates populations with different information access

faq.question: What is causing internet fragmentation?
faq.answer: Government desires for control, national security concerns, cultural values differences, economic protectionism, and data sovereignty laws. The original vision of a borderless internet conflicts with nation-states' desire to regulate their information environments.

faq.question: Does internet fragmentation affect ordinary users?
faq.answer: Yes. It determines what information you can access, which services you can use, and what legal protections apply to your data. A Chinese citizen cannot access Google. European users have GDPR protections Americans lack.
